Uniform Title: Lalleśvarīvākyāni Author: Lalleśvarī Alternate Name: Lal Ded
Commentator: Bhāskara. Description: This text is volume 26 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.
Notes: The electronic text was transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: October 15, 2007.
Publisher: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State Publication Year: 1918 Publication City: Srinagar
Country of Publication: India Oṃ,
salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now follow the words of Lalleśvarī, accompanied by Sanskrit verses composed by the venerable Rājānaka Bhāskarācārya.
Having bowed to the god Śrī Gaṇeśa, the lord of the gods, and having remembered the sandals of the venerable Guru in my heart,
[I shall present] the collection of words uttered by Lallādevī.
It is composed in verse by Bhāskara. || 1 ||
Free from expansion and contraction, the reality is like the sky; it is subtle, endowed with qualities, and all-pervading.
It is empty, yet free from disease, and self-existent.
The soldiers have received this instruction here. || 1 ||

When the visible world has been brought to dissolution through practice and has reached a state of emptiness, that which remains is the nature of the witness; even when that emptiness is stilled, it is free from all affliction.
Neither speech nor mind can reach it; neither the *kvala* nor the *akvala* can enter its seal.
Neither the sun nor Śiva-Śakti can attain it.
The instruction heard from my father’s mouth has been well-learned by me. || 2 ||
And that [state] consisting of speech and mind is the Mudrā of Śiva and Śakti, both Kula and Akula;
where all this is dissolved—that indeed is the supreme instruction.
Lalla says: "The Lord has entered my heart; I have abandoned lust and anger, whether by day or by night. I have spoken thus before the assembly of learned men."
I have heard that the host of stars has been swallowed by Rāhu. || 3 ||
I, Lallā, went far away to search for the omnipresent Lord Śaṅkara;
after wandering about, I found the God within my own body, residing right there at home.
In the festival of self-restraint, we kindle the lamp; let us not go there empty-handed. Darkness is dispelled by light; it is the very essence of splendor.
I have composed this in the Raṭuma meter. || 4 ||
Then, having kindled the lamp of knowledge by means of the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, I clearly beheld there the stainless nature of consciousness. (4)
I restrain my speech, I restrain my mind,
and I have restrained my body from night until morning; thus,
my mind is perfectly composed.
O Lord, Preceptor of the Gods, please grant me this favor. || 5 ||
He for whom self and other, day and night, and all this world are equal—by him, whose mind perceives non-duality, has the Lord of the Immortals been seen. || 5 ||
These two— liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and liberation after death (*videhamukti*)— are the fruits of the light of knowledge belonging to the bliss of consciousness;
they are the release from the snare of this poisonous worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
There are hundreds upon hundreds of boils on his body. || 6 ||
Consciousness-bliss, whose nature is knowledge, called "the Light," and free from all affliction—those by whom this is attained are liberated even while possessing a body; others remain otherwise.
O Lord, we have no food, no drink, and no other sustenance; we always subsist on this single body.
We do not eat or drink anything else; we eat only our own excrement.
The grass grows on the bank; what doubt can there be as to whose hunger it is? || 7 ||
"O Lord, neither you nor even myself were known due to the conceit of identifying with the body; because of that, there was the doubt: 'Who are the two of us? (7)
Whether it be Śiva, Keśava, or Jina— whichever name of the Lord of the Lotus-born one you utter—
the disease of existence will be cured for me.
Bliss, indeed, bliss, indeed, bliss, indeed, bliss. || 8 ||
Whether it be Śiva, Keśava, Jina, or even Druhiṇa, may he treat me—a woman overcome by the disease of saṃsāra. (8)
When the sun shines, it becomes light; when the moon shines, it becomes cool. But when the mind shines, nothing remains as it was before.
Having offered the oblation with the vyāhṛtis *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, he performed the *mīlitha* sacrifice.
When the sun has vanished, the lunar orb shines; when that too has vanished, the mind alone shines.
When the mind has vanished, the entire world of appearances vanishes in an instant.
All this, beginning with the earth, goes somewhere.
Then the son of Raṇī, Arcuna, spoke with a gentle voice: "O King, listen to these words;
for you shall attain the supreme state."
For it is indeed the syllable Śikhara, and indeed the peak of the eye, Śikhara. || 10 ||
Arise, O Śāktika woman! Worship the Lord with the gods and others;
if that Imperishable Reality has been known by you, what loss is there in that? (10)
The mantra is within the *tāya*, the *tāya* is within the mantra;
the mind is within the *galu-tāya*, and the *ke/ha* is not elsewhere.
O you who are empty, I am empty; we have met like two cows. || 11 ||
The entire tantra dissolves into mantra alone;
mantra, rooted in sound (nāda), dissolves into the mind (citta).
When the mind has dissolved, everything indeed dissolves.
The object of sight and the seer remain as the nature of consciousness alone. || 11 ||
Thus, he did not rule the kingdom again, nor did his mind find satisfaction in what he had seen;
for a living being does not die without greed.
Having died while living, one is cast off from knowledge. || 12 ||
The mind of the giver is not satisfied even by giving away a kingdom, nor is that of the receiver satisfied by having obtained it; likewise,
a living being does not escape death merely through gain.
For one who has died, there is never again death. || 12 ||
By this power and by my own power,
may the hunger and thirst of Śyāmāgalā be completely destroyed;
may there be no distinction between them.
Then the master said to his wife: "Go. || 13 ||
O Lord, that which is your sixfold [nature] is indeed mine as well, O Master; you are the employer and I am the one to be employed—this is the only distinction between us.
Śiva is the teacher, Keśava is the protector, Brahmā is the one who causes the cycle of rebirth, and Viṣṇu is the one who destroys it;
the Yogi is the rain-cloud for the seed of yoga.
Kusa, Deva, Aśvavāra, Pyaṭha, and Ceḍya. || 14 ||
Śiva is the horse, Keśava is its saddle, and likewise Ātmabhū is the foot-strap;
tell me, who is the rider fit for that? (14)
p. 7) The Unstruck (anāhata), whose nature is space, the abode of emptiness, which has no boat, no color, no form, and no lineage;
it is the resonance of "Ahaṃ," the Bindu, and the Yava.
The horseman heard the cry of the servant. || 15 ||
He is unstruck, the very nature of space, abiding in emptiness, free from ailment;
devoid of name, form, or color, unborn, he exists as the essence of Nāda and Bindu.
The water of the flute flows swiftly; indeed, the three qualities (guṇas) are here distinct and diverse in their deliberations. Yet, the resonance of consciousness shines equally throughout all.
Behold the world of moving and unmoving beings as consisting of Śiva. || 16 ||
The dullness of illusion, the water of consciousness born from it, and the ice of its density called "saṃsāra"—
these three instantly vanish when this sun of consciousness has risen.
The primordial water, freed from dullness, is called Śiva. || 16 ||
The body is a banyan tree, the husband is a banyan tree; both have become one.
O you who are like a hollowed-out banyan tree, how can you perform worship?
The union of the hand, the mind, and the vital breath. || 17 ||
The deity in the shrine and the two [images] fashioned by you for the sake of worship are not distinct from the stone;
the deity is immeasurable and consists of the nature of consciousness. This is what must be understood.
For the sake of its pervasion, there is indeed the identity of the vital breath and the mind. || 17 ||
Hope speaks, but its transformation is sorrow;
even if one dwells in a palace, there is no end to distress. O Shankara, hope is indeed a burden.
"O Makuriṣa, what did Svāsa say? Drink! || 18 ||
Let thousands of unspeakable things be told; my mind does not become stained by them, just as a mirror remains indifferent and unaffected by dust.
Having come, one goes;
having gone, one returns—whether by day or by night.
Having come from afar, one goes quickly.
What is it? What is it? What is it? What is it? || 19 ||
Old age has arrived and my body is now exceedingly worn; the time for departure has come. We have come from wherever we originated, back to that very place.
In this matter, one must certainly proceed resolutely; there is nothing else to be done. || 19 ||
p. 9) O fool, look at that and see it;
that body was once inert in nature. Whatever you say about it, speak of it as such.
The practice of one who knows reality is characterized by the constant touch of what has been heard. || 20 ||
Having known everything, remain at ease like one who is ignorant;
having heard everything, one should be as if deaf;
having seen everything, quickly become as if blind.
This practice of the reality has been proclaimed by the lords of the wise. || 20 ||
Chanting the words of the *Gāḷa*, falling prostrate, and bowing down—
this is what pleases the illustrious one.
Performing worship with the flowers of the innate nature (*sahaja-kusuma*)— [This is what pleases the illustrious one.]
Tell me, O friend, what shall I say? || 21 ||
Whether they revile me or praise me, or honor me with various beautiful flowers,
I feel neither joy nor dejection.
Established in well-being through drinking the nectar of pure awakening.
Day passes and night approaches;
where on earth or in the sky does it expand? When Rāhu swallows the moon, it is the new moon.
The worship of Śiva purifies the mind and the self. || 22 ||
When the sun known as the mind has indeed set, the night called the destruction of objects of knowledge shines forth;
the moon known as the individual soul (jīva) is dissolved in the abode of Śiva.
And Svāhā immediately devours Rāhu. || 22 ||
The mind is the essence of existence;
it is the eye of women, ever prone to anger. It does not look even at one who has been humiliated by shame.
O Tuli, Tula, Tāya, Tūlu, Nāke! || 23 ||
The mind, when agitated, appears like fire;
when suppressed, it shines as if weighed down by a burden;
yet through inquiry, it is seen to be free from all modifications.
It is indeed of the singular nature of pure awakening. || 23 ||
(11) O Śīla, you have fallen into the trap of pride; you shall engage in hand-to-hand wrestling with me.
With my fist, I shall crush your head.
Thus, O illustrious one, happiness arises from the giving of wealth. || 24 ||
The protection of one's virtue and honor can be effectively accomplished by those very same guards; yet, one cannot catch the wind with the hand nor a wild elephant with a mere thread.
which can be suppressed by those who are truly steadfast. || 24 ||
Together we shall practice the yoga of the crescent moon; we shall practice the yoga of the wind-born breath.
We shall practice the yoga of the lotus-born mind and the yoga of the lotus-stalk.
O Śaṅkara, you have become weary and exhausted. || 25 ||
Having cut down this forest of the six [senses], beginning with desire, I have attained the nectar consisting of awakening;
and through devotion and the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, I have reached primordial nature (prakṛti).
And having burned away the mind, the abode of Śiva was attained. || 25 ||
The mind, like a bird, wanders through the sky; in the blink of an eye, it traverses ten thousand yojanas.
O you who cry out with the voice of consciousness—listen!
The vital breaths, prāṇa and apāna, burst forth from his wings. || 26 ||
The horse called "mind," which traverses all realms and covers a hundred thousand *yojanas* in a single moment,
must be held by the Lord of the Wise with the bridle of discernment.
Or by means of *noda*, through the obstruction of the two wings of the vital air. || 26 ||
O Gaḍitha, your mind is not at peace;
you have wandered like one who has lost his way.
You have acted contrary to the scriptures and have violated your vows.
May we not suffer harm; may she be blessed with prosperity. || 27 ||
He whose mind is free from delusion regarding food or even ornaments is liberated; for he who does not take wealth from a creditor is indeed free from debt.
As the barley moved, so did the sky; as the skin moved, so too did her food and drink.
King Citta was satisfied by his own reflections.
What can the forest say to the body on the funeral pyre? || 28 ||

Clothing should be accepted for the sake of warding off cold, and likewise food for the sake of warding off hunger; the mind should be led toward discernment—it is enough to stop reflecting on sensual enjoyments. (28)
The innate state does not go toward tranquility or self-restraint;
it seeks the door of liberation.
Just as salt dissolves when mixed with water, so too does that [innate state] depart.
Thus, this reflection on the innate (sahaja) is difficult to attain. || 29 ||
Neither tranquility nor self-restraint is the cause for attaining one’s true nature; rather, supreme discernment is the cause—
just as salt becomes of the same form as water.
Likewise, even when unity is attained, this [state] is not obtained. || 29 ||
Greed and delusion are innate; know that they arise from conceptual construction.
Know that night and day are far removed from it.
O cow, you have closed your eyes in the midst of emptiness. || 30 ||
Having abandoned greed as well as dejection,
one should constantly practice the contemplation of one's own true nature;
for just as emptiness is not at all different from emptiness, so it is.
Therefore, your notion of their difference is entirely in vain.
(14) The multitude of people are like a mirror, yet their minds are filled with falsehood; they know only the fruit of this life.
Even as they drink the wine of night, they find no happiness.
O father, mother, sister, and brother, what shall we do? || 31 ||
When the mirror of my mind attained purity,
self-recognition arose within me;
I beheld that very Lord in His own true form.
Neither I, nor you, nor even this conceptual proliferation exists. || 31 ||
Some bathe in the waters of the Vaitaraṇī; some cross over it by means of a raft. Some bathe in the waters of the Apūpikā.
He built a house for Keśava, though he himself remained inactive. || 32 ||
One who is asleep may yet be truly awake,
while another who is awake is like one who sleeps;
one who has bathed may, in my view, still be considered impure.
And another, being well-purified, having enjoyed a woman as well. || 32 ||
The syllable *oṃ* is the navel of the unborn; the conch is within the womb of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
The unborn performs the creation of the intermediate space.
What can people do within the interval between His commands? || 33 ||
By him who has eternally held this single mantra called Oṃ within his very center as far as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
having made his mind have that [mantra] alone as its essential core of reflective awareness—
What need has he for other collections of mantras? || 33 ||
Through the austerity of the iron of saṃsāra,
the innate light of awakening is obtained;
one neither dies nor is one born.
I have no desire for death, nor do I have a longing for life. || 34 ||
Having entered this miserable cycle of existence, I have attained pure, innate awakening;
I do not belong to anyone, nor does anyone belong to me.
To me, death and immortality are of equal form. || 34 ||
The mandala of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) is the abode of that deity;
the breath of the nose is the unstruck sound (anāhata-rava). That very [deity] is established here as the limit of conceptualization.
O God, we have praised you; what [further] shall we do? 35.
He who, being Śaṅkara himself, resides within the ever-shining temple of the gods imagined at the dvādaśānta, impelling the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa); he—
Whom should that wise man worship, who has become his very self? || 35 ||
O ascetic, travel to holy places;
meet Sudarśana, the Lord of the World.
Cast away the mind’s delusion and abandon all hope.
Having gone to the distant land of Deśaka, he remained there for a long time. || 36 ||
Always possessing the singular resolve for liberation, these renunciants go with effort to the most excellent of holy places;
yet that [liberation], which is to be accomplished by the mind alone, is not attained by them.
The durvā grass field shines intensely blue from afar.
p. 17) When the wind filled the air with dust, even his eyes could not see the path;
there, his compassion was exhausted by that hardship.
One should not desire even the sovereignty over the entire cycle of existence. || 37 ||
He who restrains his own mind through inhalation (pūraka) is not afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the like within saṃsāra; his life is truly fruitful. || 37 ||
Water is the fuel for the fire; crossing over is the practice devoid of upward movement;
the twelve months are the pieces of wood.
Now, all this was merely a display of deceitful conduct. || 38 ||
A pillar made of water, the coldness of fire,
likewise traveling through the sky on foot, and similarly milking a cow made of wood— these are all impossible.
And all of this is but a manifestation of deceit.
Where shall flowers be sought? Where shall incense be burned for worship?
Where is the lake from which water shall be drawn for the ritual vessel?
O Śaṅkara, may you be pleased with this armor-mantra. || 39 ||
Who is the florist, and who is his wife?
With what flowers is the worship of the excellent deity to be performed,
and likewise, what should be made of the water-pot?
And tell me, what mantra should be employed there? || 39 ||
Offer the mind as the sacrificial animal; worship with the flowers of pure intention. Offer the nectar of the moon as the medicinal paste for the water-vessel.
O Śaṅkara, I bow to you with this mantra. || 40 ||
Having indeed taken the flower called "firm conviction" with the two hands of desire and mind,
and having offered a sugar-cube made of the floods of one's own bliss—
I worship the Lord with the mantra known as Mauna.
In which direction is my iron vessel? Where has it gone? Who knows where it has gone?
It must have fallen right here.
A hundred thousand [offerings] for each of the six nights of the dark fortnight. || 41 ||
(19) "By which direction and by which path have I come?
And by which path shall I go hereafter?
Since I do not know my own course in this way, [I am lost].
With a mere breath, I maintain my fortitude. || 41 ||
The accumulation of the sky, the accumulation of the earth, the accumulation of fire, wind, and space;
the accumulation of the moon, the sun, and the nourishment of the quarters— these are the accumulations.
What will happen when the time for the gathering of the harvest arrives? || 42 ||
Space, earth, wind, water, fire, night, and day— all these are you alone;
and because they are your effects, even flowers, the arghya offering, and so forth, are you.
For the sake of worshipping you, I have not obtained anything at all. || 42 ||
O Manmatha, you have killed me with the deer-form of greed; O Lord,
you have killed me with the bull-form of innate ignorance.
The breath flows through the left nostril for two and a half hours. || 43 ||
By that very same person who previously, with effort, killed desire, greed, and ego— the thieves on the path—
having attained the abode of the Lord, alone.
Having abandoned everything like ashes, the entire collection of existing things.
The suffering that arises from drinking liquor ceases;
by abandoning it, one will attain the state of a god.
The suffering that arises from gambling with dice ceases when one masters the treasury of knowledge.
I shall go to see the deceased father. || 44 ||
O Maheśa, having failed to reach You because You are concealed by the six sheaths beginning with the body, I have long been weary;
[I seek] Your form of pure consciousness, liberated from all limiting adjuncts.
Having known you today, they have attained rest.
Kuśa grass, nourishment, sesame, lamps, water, and incense—these are not found in the house; yet, through the true nature of the food, it is considered as if it were offered to Śiva himself.
It is indeed the very essence of Śambhu.
I offer the innate ritual action. || 45 ||
(p. 21) This substance, such as flowers and the like, is not at all useful for his worship;
rather, [it is effective] through firm devotion and the instruction of the Guru.
By means of mindfulness, the pure self is honored.
If one sleeps at dawn,
one should perform an ablution at a sacred ford; likewise,
one should eat only after having sipped water.
The night has passed for those who possess discernment. || 46 ||
Behold the God of the Self within your own very body— bathed, laughing, performing various activities, and existing right here in this city.
Enough with searching for another location! || 46 ||
Just as the essence is not found within a mustard seed, so too is the essence not found within all the five aggregates.
[The same applies to] deer, jackals, rhinoceroses, and water elephants.
Knowledge is not knowledge; it is merely a semblance of knowledge. || 47 ||
(p. 22) It is truly marvelous that in this lake not even a single grain of mustard can be contained;
yet, it increases in volume through all that water.
Indeed, for as great as the extent of the aggregate of embodied beings may be. || 47 ||
Lalla says: Abandoning the world, one should remain in the cave of the heart; there, the nectar of the supreme state flows.
Having cast away the body, one beholds the true form of the Self.
The time for my departure is now to be counted; it is the third watch of the night.
I went to the best of sacred fords to see the All-pervading Lord; I remained there, weary, chanting His praises,
yet even from that I am now exhausted in spirit.
Indeed, she is truly established within one's own heart during the contemplation of that. || 48 ||
I bow to the Mala;
Jigara is my mother.
Tyali Lalla is my father.
The third [chapter] is called "The Burning of the Forest. || 49 ||
Then, having seen the obstacles here once more,
I realized that [the goal] would be achieved right here.
And when I had broken through those [obstacles], I entered.
I am then celebrated in the world as Lalletī. || 49 ||
The three Vedas are like a lake; from that lake, the four Vedas were born.
From the mouth of Hara, the six Vedāṅgas emerged like lotuses.
When there is [the mind], its essence is the form of emptiness. || 50 ||
Three times I remember it as consisting of water, and likewise once I saw it as devoid of space; I also remember other such wonders of the sky.
I indeed remember it as empty seven times. || 50 ||
Knowing this, one should give rise to joy;
by that, one should abandon the many afflictions of the belly. One should open the door and break through the skin.
Śiva touched her head and gave her this instruction: || 51 ||
Having emerged from the mother’s womb— which is filled with afflictions—
even though born smeared with impurities, a man constantly pursues a woman, driven by her as he perceives her to be a source of happiness.
Listen, O Guru, to that auspicious [teaching] which is obtained with great difficulty. (51)
One should personally carve the pedestal for the cloth painting; one should personally carve the most excellent location.
One should personally carve the frame for the portable shrine.
Śiva touched him and gave him this instruction: || 52 ||
Just as a single stone, through the differentiation of its own kind, assumes various forms such as a pedestal and so forth,
even so does He who shines forth in infinite ways.
Listen, O Guru, to that auspicious [teaching] which is obtained with great difficulty.
According to the view of Rava, one should heat the vessel plate by plate; according to the view of Uttama, one should heat it repeatedly.
According to the view of Varuṇa, the poison is digested without thought.
Śiva gave this instruction to Krūṭutāya. || 53 ||
Just as the sun, by means of its own rays, falls without distinction upon various places, houses,
or clouds, so too does [the Light] fall upon the houses of the entire world.
Listen, O Guru, to that auspicious [teaching] which is obtained with great difficulty.
In the form of a mother, I give milk; in the form of a wife, I provide delight;
in the form of Māyā, I carry away the living soul.
Śiva touched him with his hand and gave him this instruction: || 54 ||
In the form of a mother she bestows milk;
in the form of a wife she provides pleasure;
and her power finally takes the form of death.
Listen, O Guru, to that auspicious [teaching] which is obtained with great difficulty.
Having abandoned the palace at Kandyava, he dwelt in the forest; whatever sorrow there was, that very thing became his hope.
With fortitude as his chariot and the fragrance of the *sāpājakha* flower as his seat, he proceeded.
What is touched by the sun and what is touched by the breath? || 55 ||
(p. 26) Dwelling in a house or in the forest has not been taught by the best of yogis as the cause of liberation;
rather, it is [liberation] for one who is rich in the constant self-investigation day and night.
As you exist, you are the supreme means. || 55 ||
Those who are the best of the best,
whose true nature is existence itself,
have abandoned me; just as the city of Kanda was brought forth by Jani.
Alas, when will that youth come? Alas, when will that [time] come? || 56 ||
O Guru, out of compassion, grant me this one instruction that brings about the attainment of awakening;
for these two, "Hā" and "Hūṃ," are born simultaneously from his mouth.
"O Vatsa, is it hot? Or rather, is it very cold? || 56 ||
The water residing at the site of the navel is like a lake; the cool-faced one resides at the site of Brahmā;
many rivers flow from the expanse of the cosmic egg.
By you, O youth, that [state] was indeed attained here. || 57 ||
HĀH is not arisen [from the heart], being heated by the digestive fire;
HŪH has arisen from the cool *dvādaśānta*.
HĀH is the nature of the *prāṇa*, and HŪH is the *apāna*.
Thus has the final doctrine been proclaimed by the sages. || 57 ||
Making the sound "yiha yiha," one should worship with flowers;
while reciting the mantra "rasañi," one should fix the mind there.
Thus, having gained familiarity with the body in this manner, [one attains success].
He heard the words of the Supreme Śiva. || 58 ||
Whatever action I perform, that alone I call worship;
whatever I utter, that alone is mantra; and whatever comes to pass, that likewise arises from yoga.
That very substance exists for me here as the tantra.
Neither desire nor aversion, neither object of meditation nor meditation;
all actions are effortlessly performed as if they were merely the movement of a cow’s tongue. There is no other suffering whatsoever to be pursued.
Gaya satiated hundreds of ancestors. || 59 ||
Neither I, nor you, nor any discourse whatsoever is fit for meditation here in this state of supreme peace; therefore,
no lineage or succession shines forth here.
The virtuous should cause that which is latent here to be forgotten, as if it were their own. || 59 ||
I have abandoned greed and thirst for water; I have drunk the water of knowledge, so do not speak of it.
I have made my bed in the cemetery of delusion.
He does not discharge his arrows one by one; he releases them all at once. || 60 ||

Exhausted from being solely intent on the effort of seeking my own self, I then remained in that utterly solitary, great state of the knowledge of That; thereafter, by the cessation of the vital breaths and other functions,
I entered the temple of the wine of bliss and beheld there the fullness of its treasures.
Nevertheless, even though they were full, the person who arrived there with his face turned away was made to grieve. || 60 ||
This collection of verses spoken by the illustrious Yoginī Lallā has been clearly composed here in sixty stanzas by me, Bhāskara; may it be an offering to Śiva. (1)
Thus end the sayings of Lalleśvarī, accompanied by the verse-commentary composed by Rājānaka Bhāskara.
